event: Wednesday: grey and still at dawn, the fells hidden; you and Shiv swim the buoy in thick mist.
At the buoy you tell Shiv Penhallow's green question, whose wanting?; you're still thinking.
"Whose wanting," Shiv repeats, treading water. "Yours, eejit. Whose else would it be?"
You laugh, and swallow mere, and choke; Shiv thumps your back, grinning, all the way to shore.
At breakfast there's a slip in your pigeonhole: bursar's office, two o'clock today, to sign papers.
Bea reads it over your shoulder. "That's just the bursary forms. Everyone gets one. It's dull."
Ten: Sigils in the Drawing Room; the tutor sets the mending sigil, the split line and the join.
Lin's are perfect again; yours come out loose and even, and the tutor nods as she passes.
Lin slides you a scrap of paper: a tiny drawing of a cup with a seam, and a smiling face on it.
Lunch: Kit sits with you and Bea, and asks Bea, very formally, if she is still free at six.
Bea says she's cleared her whole diary; Kit says Bea has no diary; Bea says that's beside the point.
Two: the porters' lodge, and a panelled room behind it; the bursar's clerk is brisk and elderly.
She has a file with your name on it, and a form to sign for the term's allowance: eighty a week.
"Next of kin," she says. "Your file has none. You were in the care of Calderdale council."
You sit very still. The clerk looks up over her glasses. "Until eighteen, it says. You knew that."
You say yes, because the Nala who sat here before would have; your hands are cold in your lap.
"An emergency contact, then," she says. "Anyone at all. A friend will do. Or leave it blank."
You think of the empty phone, and the room above the shop, and a girl who had nobody coming.
You write: Beatrix Lindqvist, Thornfield House, room 15. The clerk nods and blots it.
You sign for the allowance in your new careful hand; she hands you a receipt and says good day.
Outside, you sit on the low wall by the lodge in the cold, and find you're crying, a little.
For her: the girl whose life this was, who grew up with no one, and got here anyway, alone.
You say to her, under your breath, that you'll look after it. Her life. As well as you can.
You walk the shore path alone in the free afternoon, as far as the village jetty and back.
At the jetty wall where Bea kissed you, you sit a while and watch the mist lift off the water.
Back at Thornfield you knock on 15 and tell Bea about the form; just the form, and her name on it.
Bea goes quiet. "Me? As your emergency person?" You nod. She hugs you so hard your ribs creak.
"Nobody else?" she asks into your hair, careful. "Nobody," you say. Bea holds on longer.
Six: the empty Practice Hall; you and Bea on the front bench, Bea sitting astonishingly straight.
"I'm being still," Bea whispers. "I'm being so still." Kit, mid-floor, looks at her, and freezes.
Two pairs of eyes: her hand stops in the air, and stays; you say "out"; she can't, this time.
Bea, desperate to help, holds her breath so hard her face goes red, and squeaks.
Kit stares at her; then laughs, helplessly, startled; and in the laugh her breath goes out.
The glim comes on the laugh: small, then steady, between the three of you. You count. It holds.
Six. Seven. On eight Bea gasps for air and the glim goes out, and all three of you are laughing.
Kit casts it again with both of you watching, and it holds to ten. Bea claps, then claps her mouth.
"Thursday," Kit says, flushed. "Three." She looks at Bea. "Bring Lin, if she'd come."
Eight: the poetry society in the Snug; the fire, the green sofas, the third-year with silver rings.
Tonight Kit reads first. She opens her book; her knuckles whiten; she looks across at you.
You hold her eyes this time, instead of the coals; she breathes out, and reads, low and steady.
It's a short poem, about a girl learning to swim in cold water, a little at a time.
In the silence after, as the rule asks, she keeps looking at you, and you keep looking back.
Your turn: you read a short one from the battered anthology, about a lamp in a window; better.
Kit's mouth goes in at the corner. The third-year with rings murmurs, "Better," and the fire cracks.
Kit walks you back across the quad and says, at Thornfield's door, "That poem was for you."
"I know," you say. She kisses you on the step, and goes, and her ears are scarlet in the lamplight.
In 14 you take out the cheap phone from your trunk; it still has no contacts in it at all.
You knock on 15 and ask Bea for her number; she reads it out twice, and Lin's from her phone.
You type them in, slowly: Bea. Lin. Kit's you'll ask for tomorrow, in History.
You add a note for the rest: Shiv, the rock, Sundays. Kit, Hall, six.
You look at the screen: two names and a note. More than the girl before you had in this phone.
You put the phone under your pillow beside Kit's handkerchief, and turn out the lamp.
A day at Hollowmere ends.
